name: Stretch mark surgery / tummy tuck

lead: A tummy tuck (abdominoplasty) removes excess skin and fat from the abdomen and tightens the abdominal wall, giving a flatter midsection. Stretch marks lying within the removed skin, mainly below the navel, go with it.

It is usually sought after pregnancy or major weight loss, and is described as mainly cosmetic with some reconstructive benefit for skin folds and muscle separation. Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe it as a contouring operation and do not address stretch marks directly.

paras: Under general anesthesia, skin and fat are excised through a hip-to-hip incision above the pubic area, the muscle fascia is tightened and the navel repositioned. Operating time is 2 to 5 hours, and recovery takes weeks to months.

Wikipedia reports complication rates higher than many other cosmetic surgeries, including seroma, hematoma, infection, wound separation, necrosis, thick or widened scars, numbness, blood clots and anesthesia complications. Smoking, obesity and diabetes raise risk, and it leaves a hip-to-hip scar.

web.title: Stretch mark surgery / tummy tuck — Grokipedia

angle.text: Abdominoplasty removes loose abdominal skin and fat and tightens the muscle, so the midsection looks flatter and stretch marks on the removed skin go with it. People seek it after pregnancy or major weight loss, and the change is visible after healing.

lead: Abdominoplasty, commonly called a tummy tuck, is a surgical procedure that removes excess skin and fat from the middle and lower abdomen and tightens the underlying muscle and fascia.[1][2] It changes the look of the midsection directly: loose or overhanging skin is excised, a stretched abdominal wall is pulled firmer, and the navel is repositioned, giving a flatter, more defined contour. It is typically sought after pregnancy or major weight loss, including after bariatric surgery, when loose skin and stretched muscles persist despite diet and exercise.[1][2][3]

Because the skin removed is mainly below the navel, stretch marks (striae) that lie within that tissue are removed with it, which is why the operation comes up in discussions of stretch mark treatment. Stretch marks are dermal scars from skin stretching during growth, pregnancy or weight change.[4] Wikipedia notes that no treatment for established marks is clearly effective, with lasers, topical tretinoin and hyaluronic acid among the approaches tried; surgical removal as such is not covered in its stretch-marks article.[4] Marks above the navel or elsewhere stay, and may shift position when the lower skin is pulled down.

Published research on abdominoplasty centres on complications and technique rather than on striae. Wikipedia reports complication rates higher than many other cosmetic surgeries because of the extent of dissection.[2] Studies include complication analyses, trials of seroma-prevention methods, and a 2025 meta-analysis on diabetes and outcomes.[5][6][3][7]
infobox: Hip to hip, above pubic area[2]
After pregnancy or massive weight loss[1]

paras: The operation removes skin and fat from the middle and lower abdomen, plicates (tightens) the rectus abdominis fascia, and repositions the navel through a separate incision.[1][2] Wikipedia describes several variants: a complete abdominoplasty with a hip-to-hip incision above the pubic area; a partial or mini version with a smaller incision and limited dissection of lower-abdominal skin; an extended version that continues the incision to address the flanks; a high lateral tension technique that adds lateral tightening for waist definition; a floating-navel approach; and circumferential (belt lipectomy or lower body lift) surgery, often after massive weight loss.[2] Fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty, which adds a vertical excision, is also listed as a category.[1][2]

Abdominoplasty is frequently combined with liposuction, and Wikipedia lists a 'mommy makeover' as a combined session that may add breast procedures.[2] Surgeons have also described high-definition variants such as mini lipoabdominoplasty, in which liposculpture and selective fat grafting define the abdominal muscle groups.[8] Registered trials have compared lipoabdominoplasty with traditional abdominoplasty.[9]

Grokipedia describes ideal candidates as healthy adults with stable weight for at least six months, BMI typically under 30, non-smokers, no plans for future pregnancy and realistic expectations. It lists uncontrolled diabetes, severe cardiopulmonary disease and coagulopathy as contraindications and notes psychological screening for body dysmorphic disorder.[1]

Beyond cosmetic goals, reconstructive indications include chronic skin irritation or infection beneath an overhanging abdominal fold and diastasis recti (separation of the abdominal muscles).[1] A 2023 review for abdominal surgeons notes that body-contouring operations such as a tummy tuck are commonly performed after weight reduction, following bariatric surgery.[3]

Wikipedia describes stretch marks as scars in which the dermis has torn during rapid growth, pregnancy, weight or muscle gain, or hormonal change. They start reddish or purple and over time turn paler, softer and slightly sunken. Wikipedia reports that a Cochrane review found no evidence that creams or oils prevent or reduce them in pregnancy, and that no treatment is clearly effective once they have formed.[4]

In abdominoplasty, skin below the navel is excised and the remaining upper skin is advanced downward, so striae in the lower region may be removed while marks above the navel or on other body areas remain or move.[2][4] The source articles on abdominoplasty do not discuss striae removal as an outcome, and no study found examines it.[1][2]

Surgeons have published technique refinements aimed at fewer local complications. Progressive tension sutures, described in a 2000 case series, reduce dead space between tissue layers; a 2020 review says the authors' no-drain technique built on over three decades of experience.[10][11] A 2013 literature review of barbed sutures for closing long body-contouring incisions concluded they were safe and effective with complication rates similar to conventional sutures and possibly faster closure.[12] A review of seroma, a common fluid collection after the operation, addressed its prevention and treatment.[13]

Reported complications include seroma, hematoma, infection, delayed healing or wound separation, skin or fat necrosis, thickened or widened scars, numbness, asymmetry, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and anesthesia-related events.[2] Smoking, obesity, diabetes, prior abdominal surgery and combined procedures such as liposuction are listed as higher-risk factors.[2]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of fifteen studies (79,724 patients, 5,483 with diabetes) found patients with diabetes had higher odds of overall (OR 1.63), major (OR 1.44) and minor (OR 1.84) complications than those without.[7] Published case series and reviews analysing abdominoplasty complications include a 206-case university hospital review, an 86-patient series, and a review of risk factors and the safety of combined procedures.[5][6][14] A 2024 analysis of body-contouring malpractice cases has also been published.[15] A 2024 retrospective study and literature review examined perinatal outcomes of pregnancies after abdominoplasty using a US health-records network, noting limited prior literature.[16]

Roederer first recognised striae in 1773, Troisier and Ménétrier described them histologically in 1889, and Nardelli gave the first morphologically accurate descriptions in 1936.[4] For the operation, Grokipedia states that Demars and Marx performed the first recorded dermolipectomy in 1890 during an umbilical hernia repair, that Howard Kelly described abdominal lipectomy in 1899, and that Max Thorek developed an umbilicus-preserving technique in 1924.[1] Wikipedia says modern versions developed from the 1960s.[2]

Cost and travel are recurring themes in online discussion. On looksmax.org one member described weighing travel for surgery abroad, quoting prices in the thousands of dollars for jaw procedures and for a partner's body-contouring surgery.[17] Members of a T Nation forum discussing liposuction have described waiting about a year for skin to retract before deciding on skin reduction (abdominoplasty), and one reported returning to lifting two weeks after liposuction.[18] These are individual accounts, not trial findings.

Studies of abdominoplasty itself include retrospective complication analyses, a meta-analysis on diabetes, and registered trials of technique: a completed phase 4 registration of the effects of abdominoplasty and liposuction in 143 patients, a trial of Scarpa fascia and seroma after abdominoplasty in bariatric patients (46 participants), and a completed skin-sensation study in 100 post-bariatric patients.[19][20][21][7][5][6][14] These address complications, sensation and surgical technique rather than stretch mark removal. No studies found that evaluate abdominoplasty specifically as a treatment for stretch marks.

lore.intro: Online discussion of tummy tucks tends to centre on cost, travel for surgery and recovery, and on whether skin will tighten without surgery.[17][18]

claims.claim: A tummy tuck removes stretch marks on the lower abdomen.
It is worth waiting about a year after weight loss for skin to retract before deciding on surgery.
Lifters can return to training within weeks.
Surgery abroad is a cheaper route to body contouring.
Health factors such as diabetes or smoking are secondary to cost and logistics.
Drains are unavoidable after a tummy tuck.

timeline.event: Troisier and Ménétrier describe striae histologically.[4]
Demars and Marx perform the first recorded dermolipectomy.[1]
Max Thorek develops an umbilicus-preserving technique.[1]
Nardelli gives the first morphologically accurate description of striae.[4]
Modern abdominoplasty techniques begin to develop.[2]
